Methods of Instruction The CAC has adopted the following definitions of methods of instruction: Definitions for Methods of Instruction Revision of definitions in the CAC's Three Hundred and Seventh Report (October 13, 1993) Lecture: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small- group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Laboratory: In-class applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Recitation: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Studio: In-class, supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which facuity instruct, assist, and critique. 2

Seminar: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20* students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
Independent Study: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities.
Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Practicum: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice.
Includes clinics, internships, ex tern ships, student teaching, field experiences.
May include regular class meetings.
Workshop: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
Online: A course that is delivered entirely online. (CAC policy includes possibility of a required organizational session, etc.) SECTIONI Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Facuity Senate A.

Priorities for TAAC AY 2026 • Admissions • Collaboration, transparency and openness remain essential, with the focus for TAAC on understanding the admissions process rather than oversight. • Ongoing goal would be of having the Faculty Senate informed and involved so we help to support URI to be fair, competitive and successful. • With that in mind, TAAC is organizing a walkthrough with Dean Libutti to begin to learn more about the technical details of admissions processes. • Admissions team will report to the committee, providing updates and addressing concerns when/if they arise. • TAAC will input to the Faculty Senate on Admissions/Enrollment Management issues around maintaining high admissions standards, and topics like yielding high- achieving students. • An annual verbal summary will be delivered to the committee, detailing the admissions process and addressing any concerns.

Priorities for TAAC AY 2026 Advising • TAAC members have been attending the meetings of the Reimagining Advising Committee chaired by Dean Libutti • Since last January, the Re-Imagining Advising Committee, in consultation with the deans of each college, has begun sketching a new advising model which would be a hybrid model that gives the colleges more control over how advising is done in their units. This model is not fully decentralized, however, because there would still be standards across campus and other shared advising resources. No timeline for when the model would go into effect--the committee is exploring the feasibility of implementation • URI’s goals: • more advisors to improve advising ratios and the potential for a mixed advising model, where colleges could decide their own advising approach raise retention rates • model would involve the rebranding of University College into an exploration center, with advisors moving to the colleges • need for advisors with mental health and social work skills • importance of maintaining a 12-month advising system • investing in technology to enhance advising, such as AI tools for better student support.
